title: Decorator
summary: Add behavior by wrapping an object while keeping the same interface.

parts.rule: A decorator implements the same interface as one wrapped component, delegates to it, and adds behavior before or after the call. Because the wrapper is still a component, decorators can be stacked at composition time. The public contract stays stable even as logging, retry, caching, or compression is added.
parts.why: Inheritance creates a subclass for each feature combination: logged client, retrying client, logged-and-retrying client, and so on. Decorators compose those features without multiplying subclasses. The flexibility comes with two costs: call flow is less visible, and wrapper order can change the result.
parts.example: HttpClient defines send(request). NetworkHttpClient performs the real I/O. RetryClient also implements HttpClient, holds an inner client, and retries a timeout up to 3 times. MetricsClient implements the same interface, times its inner call, and records status and duration. Build MetricsClient(RetryClient(NetworkHttpClient)). If the network times out twice and succeeds on attempt 3, RetryClient makes three network calls while MetricsClient records one 240 ms logical request. Reverse the order to RetryClient(MetricsClient(NetworkHttpClient)) and the metrics layer records three separate attempts, perhaps 80 ms each. Neither order is universally correct; choose whether the metric describes a user operation or a transport attempt. A caller still receives one HttpClient and calls send() without knowing the stack. The same reasoning applies to bytes: CompressingWriter(EncryptingWriter(file)) compresses before encryption, while EncryptingWriter(CompressingWriter(file)) asks compression to process ciphertext and will usually save little space. In an interview, name the interface, draw the wrapper order, and walk one call through every layer. That shows where errors are caught and which layer observes retries.
parts.use: Use decorators for optional behavior that can surround the same operation and may appear in different combinations. Logging, metrics, retries, authorization checks, buffering, and compression are common fits. Assemble the stack in one visible composition root and test the behavior of important orderings.
parts.refuse: Do not use a decorator to change the meaning or return contract of the wrapped interface. Avoid ten-layer stacks that nobody can inspect in a debugger. If you are selecting one algorithm rather than adding behavior around a call, use strategy. If the behavior is mandatory domain logic, place it where readers can see it instead of hiding it in an optional wrapper.

body:
Rule. A decorator implements the same interface as one wrapped component, delegates to it, and adds behavior before or after the call. Because the wrapper is still a component, decorators can be stacked at composition time. The public contract stays stable even as logging, retry, caching, or compression is added.

Why it matters. Inheritance creates a subclass for each feature combination: logged client, retrying client, logged-and-retrying client, and so on. Decorators compose those features without multiplying subclasses. The flexibility comes with two costs: call flow is less visible, and wrapper order can change the result.

Worked example. HttpClient defines send(request). NetworkHttpClient performs the real I/O. RetryClient also implements HttpClient, holds an inner client, and retries a timeout up to 3 times. MetricsClient implements the same interface, times its inner call, and records status and duration. Build MetricsClient(RetryClient(NetworkHttpClient)). If the network times out twice and succeeds on attempt 3, RetryClient makes three network calls while MetricsClient records one 240 ms logical request. Reverse the order to RetryClient(MetricsClient(NetworkHttpClient)) and the metrics layer records three separate attempts, perhaps 80 ms each. Neither order is universally correct; choose whether the metric describes a user operation or a transport attempt. A caller still receives one HttpClient and calls send() without knowing the stack. The same reasoning applies to bytes: CompressingWriter(EncryptingWriter(file)) compresses before encryption, while EncryptingWriter(CompressingWriter(file)) asks compression to process ciphertext and will usually save little space. In an interview, name the interface, draw the wrapper order, and walk one call through every layer. That shows where errors are caught and which layer observes retries.

[[diagram:wrap]]

When to use. Use decorators for optional behavior that can surround the same operation and may appear in different combinations. Logging, metrics, retries, authorization checks, buffering, and compression are common fits. Assemble the stack in one visible composition root and test the behavior of important orderings.

When to refuse. Do not use a decorator to change the meaning or return contract of the wrapped interface. Avoid ten-layer stacks that nobody can inspect in a debugger. If you are selecting one algorithm rather than adding behavior around a call, use strategy. If the behavior is mandatory domain logic, place it where readers can see it instead of hiding it in an optional wrapper.
